name: Anterolateral Thigh (ALT) Flap

dominant_pedicle.artery: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery (LCFA)
dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: Lateral circumflex femoral artery (usually from profunda femoris)
dominant_pedicle.veins: Paired venae comitantes accompanying descending branch of LCFA

perforators.label: A (Proximal)
perforators.location: 5 cm proximal to midpoint of ASIS–superolateral patella line
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Often arises from transverse or oblique branch

perforators.label: B (Midpoint — Dominant)
perforators.location: Within a 3-cm radius of midpoint of line ASIS–superolateral patella
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Most constant dominant perforator (~80–85% musculocutaneous through vastus lateralis)

perforators.label: C (Distal)
perforators.location: 5 cm distal to midpoint of ASIS–superolateral patella line
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Higher rate of septocutaneous course between rectus femoris and vastus lateralis

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Drains reliably via paired venae comitantes uniting proximally near LCFA origin.
vascular_variants: Oblique branch of LCFA present in ~35% of thighs
Absence of usable perforators in ~1–5% (convert to AMT or TFL flap)

motor: Motor nerve to vastus lateralis (preserve unless harvesting functional muscle)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Lateral thigh hypoesthesia is common and well tolerated.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Variable with BMI (0.8–3.5 cm); can be harvested suprafascially or carefully thinned.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Origin of descending branch of LCFA (~8–10 cm below ASIS)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled superiorly to lower abdomen, groin, perineum, trochanter, and ischium; distally based (reverse flow) reaches anterior knee.

indications: Workhorse free flap for head & neck soft-tissue defects (oral cavity, pharynx, scalp)
Distal-third lower extremity Gustilo IIIB defects with exposed bone or hardware
Upper extremity and hand reconstruction (thinned or suprafascial)
Pedicled coverage of groin, perineal, lower abdominal wall, and trochanteric defects
contraindications: Prior extensive lateral thigh trauma or surgical violation of LCFA
Severe obesity when ultra-thin pliable resurfacing is required
advantages: Long, large-caliber vascular pedicle suitable for microsurgery
Two-team simultaneous harvest in supine position with low donor-site morbidity
Chimeric versatility (skin, fascia lata, vastus lateralis muscle, LFCN)
disadvantages: Variable perforator anatomy and steep intramuscular dissection curve
Subcutaneous bulk in high-BMI patients; skin graft needed if width >8–10 cm

donor_site.closure: Primary closure up to 8–10 cm width; STSG for wider defects.
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal when motor nerve to vastus lateralis is preserved.

technique.patient_positioning: Supine with hip slightly internally rotated.
preoperative_planning: Handheld 8-MHz acoustic Doppler along ASIS–superolateral patella line
landmarks: Intermuscular septum between rectus femoris and vastus lateralis
technique.design: Draw ASIS–superolateral patella line; mark 3-cm circle at midpoint (perforator B) and points 5 cm proximal (A) and distal (C).
harvest_steps: 1. Make medial incision first down to (or above) fascia lata to identify perforators safely.
2. Retract rectus femoris medially to expose descending branch of LCFA.
3. Perform meticulous intramuscular unroofing of musculocutaneous perforators while preserving motor nerve to vastus lateralis.
4. Complete lateral skin incision once perforator anatomy is confirmed.
5. Dissect pedicle proximally to desired length/caliber and divide cleanly.
6. Perform microvascular anastomosis at recipient site and close donor thigh over drain.
pearls: Always commit to the medial incision first so flap design can shift if perforators are eccentric.
Gently loop and protect the motor nerve to vastus lateralis.
pitfalls: Dividing a dominant oblique branch before verifying descending branch perforators.
Aggressive thinning directly around perforator entry causing paddle ischemia.

references.book: Blondeel PN et al. Perforator Flaps: Anatomy, Technique, & Clinical Applications
Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications

name: Deep Inferior Epigastric Perforator (DIEP) Flap
synonyms: Deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap

dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: External iliac artery superior to inguinal ligament
dominant_pedicle.veins: Paired venae comitantes of DIEA (SIEV preserved as backup)

minor_pedicles: Superficial inferior epigastric vessels (SIEA/SIEV — vital venous lifeboat)

perforators.label: Medial Row (Periumbilical)
perforators.location: 1–3 cm lateral and 0–4 cm inferior to umbilicus
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Superior perfusion across midline (Hartrampf/Holm zones II–III) with minimal motor nerve disruption

perforators.label: Lateral Row
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Closely associated with segmental intercostal motor nerves

vascular_anatomy.angiosome: Deep inferior epigastric angiosome (Hartrampf / Holm Zones I–IV)
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserve 5–6 cm of SIEV during initial elevation; supercharge SIEV to a second recipient vein if venous congestion develops.
vascular_variants: Moon–Taylor branching: Type I (~29%), Type II (~57%), Type III (~14%)
Superficial venous system dominance requiring SIEV supercharging

motor: Segmental intercostal motor nerves (T10–T12) — preserve to prevent bulge
sensory: Anterior cutaneous branch of T10–T12 intercostal nerve
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Infraumbilical abdominal wall numbness is expected.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Matches natural breast adipose consistency; Zone IV is routinely discarded to avoid fat necrosis.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Transferred as a free flap to internal mammary or thoracodorsal vessels for autologous breast reconstruction.

indications: Gold standard for autologous unilateral or bilateral total breast reconstruction
Delayed post-radiation breast reconstruction
Salvage after failed implant-based breast reconstruction
contraindications: Prior abdominoplasty or extensive transverse lower abdominal liposuction
advantages: Preserves rectus abdominis muscle and anterior sheath, minimizing bulge/hernia risk
Soft natural breast mound with abdominoplasty donor contour
disadvantages: Longer operative time and demanding intramuscular perforator dissection
Risk of fat necrosis or venous congestion if SIEV drainage is overlooked

donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal when motor nerves and rectus muscle are preserved.

preoperative_planning: Abdominal wall CT angiography (CTA) — gold standard
technique.design: Low transverse elliptical abdominoplasty pattern centered over optimal periumbilical perforators.
harvest_steps: 1. Make inferior incision first and carefully preserve 5–6 cm of SIEV bilaterally.
2. Elevate lateral-to-medial suprafascially until target perforators are exposed.
3. Open anterior rectus sheath around chosen perforator(s) and split muscle fibers longitudinally.
4. Trace perforators to main DIEA/DIEV pedicle while protecting crossing intercostal motor nerves.
5. Dissect pedicle toward external iliac origin; verify perfusion and discard Zone IV.
6. Anastomose to internal mammary vessels (3rd–4th rib space) and shape breast mound.
pearls: Preserve the SIEV early on every case as a venous congestion lifeboat.
Preoperative CTA dramatically shortens intramuscular dissection time.
pitfalls: Retaining poorly perfused Zone IV tissue causing firm fat necrosis.
Dividing lateral intercostal motor nerves leading to denervation bulge.

references.book: Blondeel PN et al. Perforator Flaps: Anatomy, Technique, & Clinical Applications
Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications

name: Superficial Inferior Epigastric Artery (SIEA) Flap

dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: Common femoral artery ~2–3 cm below inguinal ligament

perforators.label: SIEA Axial Entry
perforators.location: Crosses inguinal ligament near midpoint between ASIS and pubic tubercle
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Superficial to external oblique fascia; require ≥1.5 mm diameter before committing

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: SIEV is typically robust and courses medial to the artery.
vascular_variants: Absent or <1.5 mm in 30–65% — always prepare DIEP fallback

nerves.donor_numbness_note: Lower abdominal sensory loss similar to abdominoplasty.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Perfusion rarely crosses midline reliably; best for hemiabdominal breast volume.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Transferred as a free flap to internal mammary vessels.

indications: Autologous breast reconstruction when SIEA is ≥1.5 mm with strong pulsation
Patients prioritizing zero abdominal fascial violation
contraindications: SIEA absent or diameter <1.5 mm at inguinal ligament
Need for tissue crossing the abdominal midline
advantages: Zero violation of anterior rectus sheath or muscle (negligible hernia risk)
Fast harvest once adequate vessel caliber is verified
disadvantages: Shorter pedicle and higher arterial thrombosis and groin seroma rates

donor_site.closure: Standard abdominoplasty closure without fascial repair.

technique.design: Low transverse abdominal ellipse (identical to DIEP for seamless fallback).
harvest_steps: 1. Make inferior incision cautiously to expose SIEV and SIEA.
2. Confirm SIEA caliber ≥1.5 mm with pulsatile flow; otherwise convert to DIEP.
3. Dissect SIEA/SIEV proximally toward femoral vessels/saphenous bulb.
4. Elevate flap suprafascially over external oblique and anterior rectus sheath.
5. Discard poorly perfused contralateral tissue and transfer to chest.
pearls: Always consent patients for 'SIEA vs DIEP' and check caliber before committing.
pitfalls: Attempting SIEA on a <1.5 mm artery markedly increases thrombosis risk.

references.book: Blondeel PN et al. Perforator Flaps: Anatomy, Technique, & Clinical Applications

name: Transverse Rectus Abdominis Myocutaneous (TRAM) Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type III (superior and deep inferior epigastric arteries)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Deep inferior epigastric artery (free/MS-TRAM) or Superior epigastric artery (pedicled TRAM)
dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: External iliac artery (DIEA) or Internal mammary artery (SEA)

perforators.label: Periumbilical Musculocutaneous Cluster
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Multiple perforators captured en bloc with muscle cuff in MS-TRAM

vascular_anatomy.angiosome: Deep inferior & superior epigastric angiosomes (via choke vessels when pedicled)
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Free/MS-TRAM provides markedly superior venous outflow and lower fat necrosis than pedicled TRAM.
vascular_variants: Prior subcostal (Kocher) incision contraindicates ipsilateral pedicled TRAM

motor: Segmental T7–T12 intercostal nerves (sacrificed with full harvest)

dimensions.thickness_notes: Abundant soft breast volume; pedicled TRAM carries higher fat necrosis risk in Zones III/IV unless delayed.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled TRAM tunnels to ipsilateral or contralateral breast pocket; free/MS-TRAM transfers to IM or thoracodorsal vessels.

indications: Autologous breast reconstruction when multiple small perforators preclude single-perforator DIEP (MS-TRAM)
Pedicled breast reconstruction when microsurgery is unavailable or contraindicated
contraindications: Active smoking / severe obesity (high fat necrosis risk in pedicled TRAM)
advantages: Robust vascularity when capturing multiple perforators (MS-TRAM)
disadvantages: Higher abdominal wall bulge/hernia rate and rectus strength loss vs DIEP
Pedicled TRAM has higher fat necrosis rate and epigastric tunnel fullness

donor_site.closure: Anterior rectus sheath closure ± mesh reinforcement; layered abdominoplasty closure.
donor_site.functional_loss: Noticeable trunk flexion weakness with full or bilateral muscle harvest.

preoperative_planning: Consider 2-week vascular delay for high-risk pedicled TRAM
technique.design: Low transverse abdominal ellipse identical to DIEP.
harvest_steps: 1. Elevate skin paddle laterally to linea semilunaris preserving periumbilical perforators.
2. For MS-TRAM, harvest small muscle/fascia cuff around 2–4 perforators and dissect DIEA.
3. For pedicled TRAM, divide DIEA inferiorly, elevate muscle to costal margin, and tunnel beneath IMF.
4. Reinforce anterior rectus fascia with suture ± mesh.
5. Discard Zone IV, inset mound, and close donor abdomen.
pearls: MS-2 preserves medial and lateral rectus strips, lowering morbidity compared with full TRAM.
Ensure pedicled subcutaneous tunnel admits ≥4 fingers to avoid venous compression.
pitfalls: Closing anterior sheath under excessive tension without mesh below arcuate line.

references.book: Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications

name: Latissimus Dorsi (LD) Myocutaneous / Muscle Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type V (dominant thoracodorsal + secondary segmental paraspinous/intercostal)

dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: Subscapular artery (from 3rd part of axillary artery)

minor_pedicles: Posterior intercostal & lumbar paraspinous perforators (reverse LD for spine)

perforators.label: Proximal Musculocutaneous Cluster
perforators.location: 8–12 cm below posterior axillary fold, 2–4 cm medial to anterior border
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Over upper two-thirds of latissimus dorsi

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Large single thoracodorsal vein joining subscapular trunk.
vascular_variants: Reverse flow via serratus branch can sustain muscle if proximal thoracodorsal trunk was previously divided

nerves.donor_numbness_note: Mild numbness over posterior thoracic scar.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Broad, thin muscle (up to 25 × 35 cm) ideal for scalp or large extremity wounds + STSG.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled to breast, chest wall, sternum, shoulder, neck, and elbow; reverse LD reaches thoracic/lumbar spine.

indications: Pedicled breast reconstruction (± tissue expander/implant or radiation salvage)
Massive scalp, skull base, or lower-extremity wounds (free muscle + STSG)
Chest wall, shoulder, and brachial/elbow coverage; reverse LD for spine
contraindications: Prior posterolateral thoracotomy transecting muscle and pedicle
Crutch/wheelchair-dependent patients requiring shoulder adduction/extension power
advantages: Extremely reliable, large-caliber, long vascular pedicle
Enormous surface area and chimeric subscapular versatility
disadvantages: High donor-site seroma rate (20–50% without quilting sutures)

donor_site.closure: Primary closure with quilting sutures and closed-suction drains.
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal for daily living in non-crutch users.

technique.patient_positioning: Lateral decubitus with arm prepped freely.
preoperative_planning: Verify muscle contraction on resisted shoulder adduction
technique.design: Orient skin ellipse along bra-strap line or resting skin tension lines.
harvest_steps: 1. Incise skin paddle down to muscle fascia.
2. Dissect anterior border of latissimus and separate from serratus anterior (protect long thoracic nerve).
3. Identify thoracodorsal pedicle on deep anterior surface ~8–10 cm below axillary vessels.
4. Divide distal origins; release humeral tendon for extra anterior reach.
5. Divide thoracodorsal nerve in breast reconstruction to avoid animation deformity.
6. Place quilting sutures over drains to minimize seroma.
pearls: Progressive tension quilting sutures sharply cut donor back seroma rates.
pitfalls: Injuring the long thoracic nerve on serratus anterior (winged scapula).

references.book: Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications

name: Thoracodorsal Artery Perforator (TDAP) Flap

perforators.label: Main Descending Perforator
perforators.location: 8–10 cm below posterior axillary fold, 2–3 cm posterior to anterior LD border
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Occasionally septocutaneous anterior to muscle border (~20–30%)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Drains along perforator venae comitantes into main thoracodorsal vein.
vascular_variants: Direct septocutaneous perforator anterior to LD border in ~20–30%

motor: Thoracodorsal nerve — preserve intact within muscle

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thinner and more pliable than LD myocutaneous flap.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled to axilla, lateral/central breast (partial reconstruction), anterior chest wall, and proximal arm.

indications: Partial breast reconstruction (lumpectomy volume replacement)
Axillary hidradenitis or burn contracture release
Thin free fasciocutaneous resurfacing of extremities
contraindications: Prior axillary injury dividing thoracodorsal pedicle
No suitable perforator on exploration (convert to muscle-sparing LD)
advantages: Preserves latissimus dorsi muscle completely with minimal seroma risk
Very long pedicle (up to 18 cm including perforator)

donor_site.closure: Primary linear closure along bra line.

preoperative_planning: Handheld Doppler 8 cm below posterior axillary fold
technique.design: Transverse or oblique skin ellipse incorporating perforator in proximal third.
harvest_steps: 1. Make anterior incision to check for direct septocutaneous perforator.
2. Elevate suprafascially toward dominant perforator.
3. Split latissimus fibers longitudinally around perforator to descending thoracodorsal branch.
4. Protect thoracodorsal nerve throughout.
5. Tunnel pedicled flap anteriorly without twist, or divide for free transfer.
pearls: A small 2-cm muscle cuff (MS-LD) is a safe fallback if tiny perforators are encountered.
pitfalls: Twisting the long skeletonized perforator during anterior tunneling.

references.book: Blondeel PN et al. Perforator Flaps: Anatomy, Technique, & Clinical Applications

name: Gracilis Muscle / Myocutaneous Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type II (one dominant proximal pedicle + 1–2 minor distal pedicles)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Ascending branch of medial circumflex femoral artery (MCFA)

minor_pedicles: 1–2 distal segmental branches from superficial femoral / descending genicular artery

perforators.label: Proximal Third Skin Territory
perforators.location: Over proximal 1/3 of gracilis, 6–12 cm below pubic tubercle
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Distal two-thirds longitudinal skin is unreliable

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Paired venae comitantes converge near profunda femoris.

motor: Anterior branch of obturator nerve (L2–L4) — enters 1–2 cm superior to vascular pedicle

dimensions.thickness_notes: Muscle is ~25–30 cm long, 4–6 cm wide; undergoes ~30–50% denervation atrophy under STSG.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: MCFA vascular entry (~8–10 cm below pubic tubercle)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled to perineum, groin, vagina, rectovaginal fistula, ischium, and exposed femoral vessels.

indications: Dynamic facial reanimation (functional free muscle transfer)
Small-to-moderate distal lower extremity or foot defects (muscle + STSG)
Pedicled perineal, pelvic, rectovaginal fistula, and groin vascular graft coverage
Functional elbow flexion or forearm finger flexor restoration
contraindications: Prior medial thigh vascular surgery or severe profunda atherosclerosis
Need for very large surface-area coverage
advantages: Expendable muscle with negligible functional deficit
Fast, reliable harvest in supine frog-leg position (two-team compatible)
Ideal excursion and single motor nerve for facial reanimation
disadvantages: Relatively short pedicle (5–7 cm) and modest arterial caliber

preoperative_planning: Palpate adductor longus tendon at pubic tubercle
Mark line to medial tibial condyle; gracilis lies 2–3 cm posterior
technique.design: Longitudinal medial thigh incision 2–3 cm posterior to adductor longus line.
harvest_steps: 1. Incise medial thigh fascia posterior to adductor longus; confirm gracilis by tugging distal tendon.
2. Retract adductor longus anteriorly to expose MCFA pedicle 8–10 cm below pubic tubercle.
3. Dissect anterior branch of obturator nerve superomedially (up to 8–10 cm for facial reanimation).
4. Ligate minor distal pedicles and trace dominant pedicle deep to adductor longus.
5. Divide proximal/distal attachments or pivot into perineal tunnel.
pearls: Follow the pedicle deep to adductor longus to gain an extra 2 cm of length and caliber.
pitfalls: Relying on distal longitudinal skin over the lower half of the muscle.

references.book: Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications

name: Radial Forearm Free Flap (RFFF)

classification.cormack_lamberty: Type C (septocutaneous perforators in lateral intermuscular septum)

dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: Brachial artery bifurcation in cubital fossa
dominant_pedicle.veins: Paired venae comitantes AND/OR superficial cephalic vein

minor_pedicles: Retrograde palmar arch flow (reverse-flow pedicled RFFF for hand)

perforators.label: Distal Lateral Intermuscular Septum
perforators.location: Distal volar forearm between brachioradialis and FCR
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Densest perforator concentration 2–8 cm proximal to wrist crease

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Dual deep (venae comitantes) and superficial (cephalic vein) outflow linked at cubital fossa.
vascular_variants: Incomplete palmar arch — MANDATORY preoperative modified Allen test

sensory: Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve (LABCN) for sensate flap
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Protect superficial radial nerve to prevent dorsal first webspace numbness/neuroma.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Ultra-thin, pliable, relatively hairless volar skin — gold standard for oral cavity and phalloplasty.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Wrist crease / palmar arch (reverse pedicled) or free transfer
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Reverse-flow pedicled RFFF reaches dorsal/volar hand and thumb; free flap reaches anywhere.

indications: Oral cavity (tongue, floor of mouth, soft palate) and hypopharyngeal reconstruction
Thin pliable resurfacing of hand/wrist (reverse pedicled) or distal foot
Total phalloplasty (sensate tube-within-a-tube)
contraindications: Abnormal modified Allen test or ulnar artery insufficiency
Prior radial arterial line trauma or dialysis AV fistula in donor arm
advantages: Ultra-thin, pliable tissue with consistent anatomy and long large-caliber pedicle
Dual venous outflow and reliable sensate potential via LABCN
disadvantages: Sacrifices radial artery; conspicuous forearm donor site requiring skin graft
Risk of FCR tendon exposure if paratenon is stripped

donor_site.closure: STSG/FTSG over intact paratenon with wrist splint for 7–10 days.
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal when FCR paratenon is preserved.

technique.patient_positioning: Supine, non-dominant arm on hand table under tourniquet.
preoperative_planning: Mark cephalic vein and radial pulse
technique.design: Center paddle over distal radial artery axis on volar forearm.
harvest_steps: 1. Confirm normal modified Allen test and inflate tourniquet.
2. Elevate ulnar-to-radial suprafascially preserving FCR paratenon up to lateral septum.
3. Elevate radial-to-ulnar preserving superficial radial nerve.
4. Clamp and verify ulnar backflow before ligating radial artery at wrist.
5. Dissect radial vessels, cephalic vein, and LABCN proximally.
6. Deflate tourniquet, verify perfusion, divide pedicle, and skin-graft donor bed.
pearls: Suprafascial elevation dramatically lowers FCR tendon exposure.
pitfalls: Stripping paratenon off FCR tendon or injuring superficial radial nerve.

complications: Donor graft loss / FCR tendon exposure

references.book: Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications
